explanations.explanation: Bethsaida is the destination, baker. Mark says Jesus made His disciples get into the boat and go on ahead of Him to Bethsaida, while He dismissed the crowd (Mark 6:45). The boat had a heading before it ever left the shore. That's more planning than I did for my last batch, and I had a recipe card.

Close, friend, but Mark doesn't name Capernaum here. He says Bethsaida. "…go on ahead of Him to Bethsaida…" (Mark 6:45). I mix up my toppings jars the same way, so no shame. Just keep Bethsaida in your pocket for this one.

Tiberias is a fine name, but it isn't in this passage. Mark says the disciples were to go on ahead of Jesus to Bethsaida (Mark 6:45). Sometimes a stamp comes out a little smudged, and that's okay. The right answer is sitting right there to give you a clean press.

Yes, baker. Mark says Jesus made His disciples get into the boat and go on ahead of Him, "…while He dismissed the crowd." (Mark 6:45). So they go first, and He stays behind on land. I've sent a batch ahead of me to the cooling rack plenty of times, but never with this much on the line.

It's actually True, friend. Mark 6:45 says Jesus made His disciples get into the boat and go on ahead of Him to Bethsaida, while He dismissed the crowd. So He stays on land while they head out. If you missed it, join the club, because I once missed a whole oven timer.

Pray it is. Mark says that after bidding them farewell, Jesus "…went up on the mountain to pray." (Mark 6:46). Crowd gone, boat gone, and He heads up to pray. I think that's a good reminder to have a quiet place of your own, even if mine is the pantry.

Sleep sounds reasonable, friend, and I've taken that nap myself, but it's not what Mark says. He says Jesus went up on the mountain to pray (Mark 6:46). Nothing about a pillow or a blanket there. Pray is the word that fits the blank.

Fast is a good guess, baker, but Mark doesn't say it here. The text says Jesus went up on the mountain to pray (Mark 6:46). No mention of skipping a meal on that mountain. The blank wants "pray," and now you've got it.

Right, baker. Mark says Jesus "…could see that the disciples were straining to row, because the wind was against them." (Mark 6:48). The wind is pushing one way and they're pulling the other. I get tired just stirring a heavy batch, so I feel for them.

explanations.answer: The boat is taking on water
explanations.explanation: That would be a problem, friend, but Mark doesn't say it. The reason he gives is that the wind was against them (Mark 6:48). He says nothing about a leak. I'd rather bail out a mixing bowl than a boat anyway.

explanations.answer: One of the oars has snapped
explanations.explanation: A snapped oar would be rough, but it's not in the text, baker. Mark says they were straining to row because the wind was against them (Mark 6:48). The wind is the reason he gives, and he says nothing about an oar breaking.
Walking, baker! Mark says Jesus went out to them "…walking on the sea." (Mark 6:48). Not sailing, not swimming. I can barely walk across my kitchen without my base sliding, so this stops me cold.

Sailing makes sense for a lake, friend, but there's no boat under Jesus here. Mark says He went out to them walking on the sea (Mark 6:48). The disciples are the ones in the boat. Jesus is on top of the water on His own two feet.

Swimming is a fair guess, baker, but Mark says something bigger. Jesus went out to them "…walking on the sea." (Mark 6:48). No splashing, no strokes. Just walking, and that's the word that goes in the blank.

Ghost is right, baker. Mark says that when they saw Him walking on the sea, "…they cried out, thinking He was a ghost…" (Mark 6:49). Think about it from their seat in the boat. A figure on the water in the dark is going to get a loud reaction from anybody, and I'd have yelled too.

A stranger would be scary enough, friend, but that's not what Mark says. They cried out, "…thinking He was a ghost…" (Mark 6:49). They didn't think someone was walking by. They thought something far spookier was out there. I'd have dropped my spatula.

Angel is a nice thought, baker, but it's not what they thought. Mark says they cried out, "…thinking He was a ghost…" (Mark 6:49). Nobody cries out in joy there. It was a cry of fright, and ghost is the word the text gives.

It's actually False, baker. Mark says "…they all saw Him and were terrified." (Mark 6:50). So it wasn't just a couple of them seeing things. The whole boat saw the same thing, and the whole boat was scared.

False is right, friend. Mark says "…they all saw Him and were terrified." (Mark 6:50). Nobody had to say "did you see that?" because everyone in the boat already had. If it were just one person, they might have blamed the dark. With everybody seeing it, that excuse is gone.

explanations.answer: It's Me so don't be afraid
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. Jesus says, "Take courage! It is I. Do not be afraid." (Mark 6:50). Mark says He spoke up at once. Hearing a voice you know right when you're scared is a gift.

That sounds like a coach, friend, but it's not what Jesus says. He tells them, "Take courage! It is I. Do not be afraid." (Mark 6:50). Rowing harder isn't in His words. He tells them to take courage, and He tells them who He is.

Turning back isn't in the text, baker. Jesus says, "Take courage! It is I. Do not be afraid." (Mark 6:50). No new directions, just those words to calm them down. I'd take those words over a map any day.

It's the other way around, baker. Mark says that when Jesus climbed into the boat with them, "…the wind died down." (Mark 6:51). They'd been straining against it, and then it quieted. Easy mix-up when the wind is the loud part of the story.
False is right, friend. Mark says Jesus climbed into the boat with them, "…and the wind died down." (Mark 6:51). After all that straining, the wind dies down instead of picking up.

The loaves, baker. Mark says the disciples were utterly astounded, "…for they had not understood about the loaves…" (Mark 6:52). That points back to the feeding of the crowd just before this (Mark 6:41-44). Mark names the loaves as the thing they hadn't understood.

The crowd is in the story, friend, but it's not what Mark names. He says they "…had not understood about the loaves…" (Mark 6:52). The crowd got sent away, and the loaves are the thing the disciples hadn't understood. Mark picks a specific thing, and that's the one.

The mountain is where Jesus went to pray, baker (Mark 6:46), but it isn't what Mark points to here. He says the disciples "…had not understood about the loaves…" (Mark 6:52). Mark is looking back at the loaves, not up at the mountain. A small mix-up, and the loaves are the answer.

True, baker. Mark says the disciples had not understood about the loaves, "…but their hearts had been hardened." (Mark 6:52). It's a plain, honest line about these men. I think it's a good reminder that even people who walked with Jesus had things to learn.
It's True, friend. Mark says "…their hearts had been hardened." (Mark 6:52). The writer says it straight, and so do I. It's not a gotcha, just what Mark wrote about the disciples in that boat.
True, baker. Mark says that "As soon as they got out of the boat, the people recognized Jesus" (Mark 6:54). There's no waiting around and no wondering who He was. They knew Him right away.

It's actually True, friend. Mark 6:54 says that as soon as they got out of the boat, the people recognized Jesus. It happens right away, with no slow warm-up. I've been wrong about this kind of thing before, so no worries.

The sick on mats, baker. Mark says the people "…ran through that whole region, carrying the sick on mats to wherever they heard He was." (Mark 6:55). They carried people who needed help straight to Jesus. That's a lot of running and a lot of carrying.

Bread and fish were part of the feeding of the crowd earlier in the chapter, friend (Mark 6:41-44). But here, Mark says they carried "…the sick on mats…" (Mark 6:55). The people came to Jesus carrying those who needed healing. Good memory, though.

Oil and wine aren't in this passage, baker. Mark says they ran through the region "…carrying the sick on mats…" (Mark 6:55). Their hands were full of people, not presents. It's a pretty clear picture once you see it.
Yes, baker. They begged Him "…just to let them touch the fringe of His cloak." (Mark 6:56). Just the edge, nothing more. And Mark says all who touched Him were healed.

The boat is in this story, friend, but it's not what they asked to touch. Mark says they begged Him "…just to let them touch the fringe of His cloak." (Mark 6:56). The edge of His cloak is the answer.

A staff isn't mentioned in this passage, baker. Mark says they begged Him "…just to let them touch the fringe of His cloak." (Mark 6:56). The cloak's edge is the answer. It's a small thing to ask for, and they asked for just that much.
It's the other way around, baker. Mark says "…all who touched Him were healed." (Mark 6:56). He doesn't say some. He says all. That's a big word, and Mark uses it.
False is right, friend. Mark says, "And all who touched Him were healed." (Mark 6:56). Not some, not most, but all. Villages, towns and countrysides, and that word covers them all.
